title: Linux basics: the shell and services
goals: Move around the file system and copy, move and delete files from the shell
Install and update software with apt
Check, restart and read the log of a service with systemctl and journalctl
Connect to another machine with ssh and copy files with scp
summary:
The **shell** (terminal) takes typed commands. Linux runs most servers, every Raspberry Pi, and many HMIs and gateways.

**Where you are**: `pwd` prints the folder; `ls` lists it (`ls -l` with details); `cd folder` goes in, `cd ..` up one, `cd ~` home. Paths starting `/` are **absolute** (from the top); others are **relative** to where you are. Linux uses `/`, and names are case-sensitive.

**Files**: `cp a b` copies, `mv a b` moves or renames, `mkdir d` makes a folder, `rm f` deletes (no recycle bin; `rm -r` deletes a folder and everything in it), `cat f` shows a file, `nano f` edits one (Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X quits). **Tab** completes names; **↑** recalls commands; **Ctrl+C** stops one.

**sudo** runs one command as the administrator (root). Use it only when needed: files root creates are root's.

**Permissions**: read (4), write (2), execute (1) for the owner, the group and others. `rw-r--r--` is **644** (normal files); `rwxr-xr-x` is **755** (programs, folders). Set with `chmod 644 file`.

**Software**: `sudo apt update` refreshes the list of packages; `sudo apt upgrade` installs newer versions; `sudo apt install name` adds one.

**Services** (systemd): `systemctl status name` (running? latest log lines), `sudo systemctl restart name`, `sudo systemctl enable name` (start at boot). `journalctl -u name` shows its full log; add `-f` to follow it live.

**Remote**: `ssh user@host` opens a shell on another machine; `scp file user@host:folder/` copies a file to it.

bench.task: On your Raspberry Pi (over ssh), look after the Daybook service by hand.
check: `journalctl -u daybook -n 20`: read the last 20 lines of its log
`ls -l ~/Daybook/data`: who owns the databases? (you, not root)
`df -h`: how much space is left on the SD card?
`sudo systemctl restart daybook`, then status again

cards.q: In your Daybook folder on the Pi you type `rm -r data` and press Enter. What happens?
options: The data folder and everything in it is deleted for good
The data folder moves to a recycle bin
Linux asks you to confirm first
Nothing: rm only works on single files
cards.why: rm deletes straight away: no recycle bin, and by default no question. `-r` (recursive) takes the folder and everything inside. That is why backups go somewhere else, and why it pays to read a command before pressing Enter.

cards.title: Where am I? Paths
cards.body:
The shell is always **in** a folder (the working directory).

- `pwd` prints where you are; `ls` lists what is there.
- `cd Daybook` goes into a folder; `cd ..` goes **up** one; `cd ~` (or just `cd`) goes **home**, your own folder, such as /home/will.
- A path starting with `/` is **absolute**: from the very top. Any other path is **relative** to where you are.

Linux uses **forward slashes**, and names are **case-sensitive**: `Data` and `data` are different.
cards.more:
Think of the file system as a building. / is the front door; /home is the corridor of offices; /home/will is your office. pwd says which room you are in.

From /home/will, `cd Daybook` walks into /home/will/Daybook (relative: from here). `cd /etc` walks to /etc wherever you are (absolute: from the front door).

`..` is the room you came from: from /home/will/Daybook/data, `cd ../..` is back to /home/will.

Press **Tab** while typing a name and the shell finishes it for you: quicker, and no typos.

cards.q: You are in /home/pi/Daybook/data. You type `cd ../web`. Where are you now?
cards.why: `..` goes up one, to /home/pi/Daybook, then into web from there. A path not starting with / is relative to where you are.

cards.title: Working with files
cards.body:
- `cp report.csv backup.csv`: copy
- `mv old.txt new.txt`: move, or rename
- `mkdir logs`: make a folder
- `rm file`: delete. **No recycle bin.** `rm -r folder` deletes a folder and everything in it.
- `cat file`: show a short file; `less file`: page through a long one (q quits)
- `nano file`: edit; **Ctrl+O** saves, **Ctrl+X** quits

**↑** brings back earlier commands; **Ctrl+C** stops one that is running.
cards.more:
Most commands are short for what they do: cp copy, mv move, rm remove, mkdir make directory.

Before any rm, run `ls` with the same name first: `ls old*` shows exactly what `rm old*` would delete. The * matches anything, so `rm *.log` deletes every file ending .log in the folder.

cp onto a name that exists overwrites it silently; `cp -i` asks first.

nano shows its keys along the bottom; ^ means Ctrl. On Windows you would use Notepad; on a Pi over ssh, nano is the Notepad.

cards.q: Match each command with what it does.
pairs: Lists the files in a folder
Deletes a file, with no undo

cards.title: sudo: the administrator, one command at a time
cards.body:
Normal users can change their own files and nothing else. **root** is the administrator and can change anything.

`sudo` runs **one** command as root, after your password: `sudo apt install git`.

Use it only where needed: installing software, editing system settings, managing services. Anything a command **creates** under sudo belongs to **root**, so a program you later run as yourself may not be able to open it.
cards.more:
It is like a site's permit to work: you get the authority for one job, then hand it back.

The classic trap: `sudo python3 daybook.py password` creates or changes the database as root. Next time the service starts as your own user, it cannot write to its own database. That is why the Daybook instructions say to run `password` as yourself, and only the `install --service` step with sudo.

If it has happened, `sudo chown -R will:will ~/Daybook/data` hands the files back (with your own user name).

cards.q: Why should a program's data files not be created with sudo, if the program normally runs as your own user?
options: They would belong to root, and your user could not write them
sudo files are hidden from the ls command
sudo makes files read-only for everyone
sudo files are deleted when you log out
cards.why: Files are owned by whoever creates them. Created under sudo, they are root's, so when the program runs as you it gets 'Permission denied'.

cards.title: Permissions: rwx and the numbers
cards.body:
`ls -l` shows each file's permissions, such as `-rw-r--r--`. After the first character (- for a file, d for a folder) come three groups of three:

- the **owner**, the **group**, **others**
- **r** read, **w** write, **x** execute (run it, or enter the folder)

As numbers, r = 4, w = 2, x = 1, added per group: `rw-r--r--` is **644**, the usual for files; `rwxr-xr-x` is **755**, for programs and folders. `chmod 600 secret.key` makes a file private to you.
cards.more:
Add up each group of three on its own:

- rw- is 4 + 2 + 0 = 6
- r-- is 4
- r-x is 4 + 0 + 1 = 5

So `rwxr-x---` is 7, 5, 0: 750. The owner can do everything; the group can read and run it; others nothing.

Why 755 for folders? Without x you cannot go into a folder, even if you can read its list of names.

SSH refuses to use a private key file that others can read: that is what chmod 600 on it fixes.

cards.q: Permissions `rwxr-x---` as a three-digit number (read 4, write 2, execute 1)?
cards.why: Each group of three adds up on its own: owner 7, group 5, others 0.
cards.hint: Add 4, 2 and 1 for each letter present, one group at a time.

cards.title: Installing software: apt
cards.body:
Raspberry Pi OS and Debian install software from **packages** with `apt`:

- `sudo apt update`: refresh the list of what is available (it installs nothing)
- `sudo apt upgrade`: install newer versions of what you have
- `sudo apt install git`: add a package
- `sudo apt remove name`: take one off

Update first, so apt knows about the latest versions. Upgrade regularly: most security fixes come this way.
cards.more:
apt is like an app store, run from the shell. `update` is like refreshing the shop's catalogue; `upgrade` is buying the new versions of what you already own.

Forget `update` and `install` may fetch an old version, or fail because the old version has been removed from the server.

On a Pi Zero, `apt upgrade` can take a long while: let it run. If the ssh connection drops, reconnect and run it again; it carries on.

cards.q: Put these in order to install git on a fresh Pi.
cards.why: Refresh the package list, install, then check.

cards.title: Services: systemctl and journalctl
cards.body:
A **service** is a program that runs in the background from boot, such as Daybook on a Pi. **systemd** looks after them:

- `systemctl status daybook`: running or not, and its latest log lines
- `sudo systemctl restart daybook` (or `start`, `stop`)
- `sudo systemctl enable daybook`: start it at every boot
- `journalctl -u daybook`: its whole log; `-n 50` the last 50 lines; `-f` follow it live (Ctrl+C to stop)

When a service will not start, the reason is nearly always in its log.
cards.more:
Think of systemd as the shift supervisor: it starts the machines in the morning, restarts one that trips, and keeps a logbook.

`status` is the quick look: a green 'active (running)' or a red 'failed', plus the last few log lines. `journalctl -u` is the full logbook for that one service.

**enable** and **start** are different: start runs it now; enable makes it start at the next boot. After installing a service you usually want both: `sudo systemctl enable --now daybook`.

A common mistake is editing a service's file and forgetting `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, so systemd still uses the old version.

cards.q: After a reboot, a service you started by hand yesterday is not running. What was missed?
cards.why: start runs a service now; enable makes systemd start it at boot. `enable --now` does both.

cards.title: ssh and scp: working on another machine
cards.body:
`ssh will@daybook.local` opens a shell on the Pi from your PC (Windows 10 and 11 have it in PowerShell). Everything you type then runs **on the Pi**, until `exit`.

`scp` copies files over the same connection:

- `scp report.csv will@daybook.local:Daybook/` copies to the Pi
- `scp will@daybook.local:Daybook/temps.png .` copies back here (`.` means this folder)

`-r` copies a whole folder.
cards.more:
ssh is a secure remote control: the screen is the Pi's, the keyboard is yours. The prompt changes to show which machine you are on: check it before typing rm.

The part after the colon in scp is a path on the remote machine, relative to your home folder there unless it starts with /. Leave the colon off and scp thinks you mean a local file with an odd name.

On a Pi with Tailscale, the Tailscale name works the same way as daybook.local, from anywhere.

cards.q: From your PC, which command copies backup.db from the Pi's Daybook folder to the folder you are in?
cards.why: scp copies from the first place to the second. The remote side is written user@host:path, and `.` is here. The second option copies the other way.

cards.q: After an update, Daybook on the Pi does not come up. Find out why.

steps.show: `systemctl status daybook` shows 'failed', with a few log lines
`ls -l ~/Daybook/data` shows suite.db owned by root: something was run with sudo
`sudo chown -R will:will ~/Daybook/data`, then `sudo systemctl restart daybook` and `systemctl status daybook`: active (running)

cards.why: Status, log, cause, fix, check. The log almost always names the problem; the fix is checked by looking at status again.

cards.q: Why read the service's log (step 2) before trying fixes?
cards.context: journalctl -u daybook -n 50 ended with a PermissionError on suite.db.
cards.model: The log says what actually went wrong, so the fix goes straight at the cause. Without it you would guess: reinstall, reboot, change settings, each taking time and some making things worse. Here the last line named a permission error on one file, which pointed to ownership, and ls -l confirmed it in seconds.
points: The log names the actual error
Guessing wastes time and can do harm
Confirm the cause before fixing it

cards.q: Update Daybook on the Pi from git and check it came back.

steps.show: `systemctl status daybook`, and if it is not running, `journalctl -u daybook -n 50`

cards.why: Change, restart, check: never assume a restart worked.

cards.q: A file of passwords must be readable and writable by its owner only. Which command?
cards.why: 600 is rw------- : owner read and write, nobody else anything. 644 lets everyone read it; 777 lets everyone change it.

cards.q: Setting up Daybook on a fresh Pi. One line will cause trouble later. Which?
cards.why: Run with sudo, the password step creates the data folder and databases as root, and the service (which runs as you) cannot write them. Only the install step needs sudo, because it writes into /etc/systemd.

cards.q: Which command shows how much space is left on the SD card?
cards.why: df (disk free) with -h for human-readable sizes. free -h shows memory, not disk; top shows running programs.

cards.q: A file shows `-rw-rw-r--` in ls -l. What is that as a three-digit number?
cards.why: The first character (-) just says it is a file; then owner, group, others.
cards.hint: Skip the first character, then add 4, 2, 1 per group.

cards.q: You want to watch Daybook's log live while you use it from your phone. Which command?
cards.why: -u picks the service and -f follows new lines as they come (Ctrl+C to stop). status shows only the last few lines once; journalctl -n 50 without -u shows the whole system's log.

cards.q: You type `cd daybook` and get 'No such file or directory', though `ls` shows a folder called Daybook. Why?
options: cd needs the full path every time
The folder is hidden from cd
You need sudo to enter folders
cards.why: daybook and Daybook are different names on Linux. Tab completion avoids it: type `cd Day` and press Tab.

cards.q: Match each Windows habit with its Linux equivalent.
cards.why: Same jobs, different names. And Linux uses forward slashes and is case-sensitive.

cards.q: You ssh into the Pi and type `python3 daybook.py password`. Where does it run, and which Daybook does it change?
options: On the Pi: the Pi's Daybook
On the PC: the PC's Daybook
cards.why: Over ssh, everything you type runs on the remote machine until you type exit. Check the prompt shows the Pi's name before changing anything.

cards.q: A shared folder should let its owner do everything, its group read and enter it, and others nothing. What chmod number?
cards.work: owner rwx = 7; group r-x = 5 (x to enter a folder); others --- = 0: 750
cards.why: Entering a folder needs x as well as r: without x, the group could list the names but not open anything inside.

cards.q: What does `rm -r old_logs` do?
options: Deletes old_logs and all inside it, for good
Moves old_logs and all inside it to the bin
Renames old_logs to a backup name
cards.why: rm deletes, -r takes the folder and its contents, and there is no undo.

cards.q: `rwxr-xr-x` as a three-digit number?
Match each command with what it does.
pairs: Is it running? Its last few log lines
Stop it and start it again

cards.q: What does `sudo apt update` do?
options: Refreshes the list of available packages
cards.why: update only refreshes the list; upgrade installs the newer versions.
